subjects.title: The Milky Way
subjects.summary: A vast spiral galaxy containing our Sun, billions of other stars, and worlds yet to be explored.
subjects.description: The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains our Solar System. Seen from Earth as a pale band across a dark sky, it is a complex system of stars, gas, dust and dark matter. Our view from within makes mapping its full structure a remarkable scientific challenge.
facts: The Solar System lies in a region called the Orion Arm, or Local Spur.
The galaxy contains more than 100 billion stars, although estimates vary.
Its central region hosts a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A*.

sources.title: Apocalypse When? Hubble Casts Doubt on Certainty of Galactic Collision

subjects.title: Black Holes
subjects.summary: Regions of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing—not even light—can escape from within the event horizon.
subjects.description: A black hole is not really a hole. It is a huge concentration of matter packed into a very tiny space — so dense that beneath its boundary, the event horizon, gravity allows nothing to escape, not even light. Black holes themselves are invisible, but they betray themselves constantly: through the glowing matter falling toward them, the stars that orbit them, the light they bend, and the ripples they send through spacetime when they collide. They range from a few times the Sun's mass to monsters tens of billions of times heavier, and one sits at the centre of nearly every large galaxy — including our own.
facts: A black hole is a huge concentration of matter packed into a very tiny space — so dense that at its boundary, the event horizon, gravity is strong enough that nothing, not even light, can escape. The event horizon is a boundary, not a solid surface.
One kind of black hole is born when a massive star runs out of fuel and explodes as a supernova, leaving a collapsed core behind.
Most Milky Way-sized galaxies have a monster black hole at their centre. Ours is called Sagittarius A*: it is 4 million times the Sun's mass and about 27,000 light-years away.
The most massive black hole observed, TON 618, is about 66 billion times the Sun's mass. The lightest known black hole is only 3.8 times the Sun's mass.
The nearest known black hole, Gaia BH1, is about 1,500 light-years away.

Black holes neither emit nor reflect light, so astronomers detect them by their effects — glowing rings of gas and dust called accretion disks, stars orbiting something invisible and massive, light bent by their gravity, and ripples in spacetime itself.

The Event Horizon Telescope linked eight radio observatories into a single Earth-sized virtual telescope, releasing the first image of a black hole — M87*, in a galaxy 55 million light-years away — in 2019, and the first image of Sagittarius A* in 2022.

On 14 September 2015, LIGO made the first direct detection of gravitational waves: ripples from two black holes of about 29 and 36 times the Sun's mass merging 1.3 billion years ago. About three Suns' worth of mass was converted into gravitational waves in a fraction of a second.

sections.heading: Born in a collapsing star — and grown ever since
sections.body: A stellar black hole starts with a death. When a massive star runs out of fuel it can explode as a supernova, and what remains of its core collapses into an extraordinarily dense object. From there, black holes grow: by pulling in gas and dust, and by merging with other black holes — the collisions LIGO now listens for. The giants are harder to explain. Supermassive black holes of millions to billions of solar masses sit at the centres of most large galaxies, and exactly how they grew so large is still an active question: the Event Horizon Telescope team notes that how gas behaves around supermassive black holes is not yet fully understood, even though that process is thought to be a key part of how galaxies form and evolve.

sections.heading: Photographing the unphotographable
sections.body: You cannot see a black hole — it is completely dark. What the Event Horizon Telescope images is the glowing gas around one: a dark central region, called the shadow, surrounded by a bright ring of light bent by the black hole's gravity. To capture something that appears in our sky about the size of a donut on the Moon, the collaboration linked eight radio observatories across the planet into a single Earth-sized virtual telescope, and more than 300 researchers from 80 institutes spent five years combining and analysing the data with supercomputers. Sagittarius A* was the harder portrait: its gas completes an orbit in mere minutes, so its appearance kept changing during the observations, while the larger M87* takes days to weeks per orbit. The size of Sagittarius A*'s ring matched the predictions of Einstein's general relativity.

sections.heading: A common misconception: the cosmic vacuum cleaner
sections.body: Black holes do not suck things in. NASA puts it directly: they are not cosmic vacuum cleaners, and from far enough away a black hole's gravity behaves just like that of any other object of the same mass. If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of exactly the same mass, the planets would stay in their orbits — the solar system would get much colder and darker, but it would not be pulled in. A black hole is only dangerous to things that come very close: matter that strays near the event horizon can be squeezed horizontally and stretched vertically, an effect scientists genuinely call spaghettification. Nor are black holes wormholes or portals — they offer no shortcut to another place or universe.

sections.heading: An open question: what happens to what falls in?
sections.body: Nobody knows what matter looks like inside an event horizon — no observation can reach past that boundary, and NASA lists it among the things we simply do not know about black holes. Theory makes it stranger. Stephen Hawking showed that black holes are not perfectly black: they leak radiation, now called Hawking radiation, and slowly evaporate over eons. That raised a problem Hawking himself became famous for: if a black hole evaporates away, is the information about everything that fell into it lost forever — which would violate fundamental laws of physics? Hawking wagered on information loss with Caltech's Kip Thorne and John Preskill, and eventually conceded he had been wrong. But how information survives, exactly, is still unresolved — one of the sharpest open problems in the struggle to unify gravity with quantum mechanics.

sources.title: Astronomers Reveal First Image of the Black Hole at the Heart of Our Galaxy
LIGO Opens New Window on the Universe with Observation of Gravitational Waves from Colliding Black Holes

subjects.title: Orion Nebula
subjects.summary: A nearby region of gas and dust where new stars are forming, visible as a fuzzy patch in Orion's sword.
subjects.description: The Orion Nebula is one of the best-studied stellar nurseries in the sky. Inside its glowing clouds, young stars illuminate surrounding gas while dense pockets of material continue to collapse and form stars and planetary systems.
facts: It can be seen with the naked eye under dark skies.
Its young stars help scientists study how planetary systems develop.
The nebula is about 1,500 light-years away, within the Milky Way.

subjects.title: Mars
subjects.summary: A cold desert world with ancient river-like landscapes and clues to a wetter past.
subjects.description: Mars is a cold, dusty desert world with a very thin atmosphere, seasons, polar ice caps, extinct volcanoes and the largest canyon in the Solar System. It was not always so: billions of years ago Mars was warmer and wetter, with rivers, lakes and a thicker atmosphere. Today, robotic orbiters, landers and rovers investigate how the planet changed — and whether the environments it once had could ever have supported microbial life.
facts: Mars is about half Earth's size — its radius is about 3,390 kilometres — and it orbits on average 228 million kilometres (1.5 AU) from the Sun.
A Martian day, called a sol, lasts 24.6 hours, and a Martian year lasts 687 Earth days.
Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in the Solar System; its base covers an area about the size of Arizona.
Valles Marineris, the largest canyon system in the Solar System, stretches about 3,870 kilometres — more than 10 times longer and wider than Earth's Grand Canyon.
Its two small, potato-shaped moons, Phobos and Deimos, may be captured asteroids. Phobos is slowly moving toward Mars and will crash into it or break apart in about 50 million years.

Ancient river-valley networks, deltas and lakebeds show that liquid water once flowed on Mars. Today its water is found mainly as ice, because the atmosphere is too thin for liquid water to last on the surface.
Mars has distinct seasons, because its axis is tilted 25 degrees — close to Earth's 23.4 degrees — but its seasons vary in length because its orbit is noticeably elliptical.

NASA's Perseverance rover landed in Jezero Crater, an ancient lakebed, on 18 February 2021. Its passenger, the Ingenuity helicopter, became the first aircraft to achieve powered, controlled flight on another planet and completed 72 flights.

sections.heading: A world that used to be wetter
sections.body: Mars was not always a frozen desert. NASA missions have found extensive evidence that early Mars was much wetter and warmer, with a thicker atmosphere. River-valley networks, deltas and lakebeds survive on the surface, along with rocks and minerals that could only have formed in liquid water, and some features suggest huge floods about 3.5 billion years ago. Jezero Crater tells the story in one place: more than 3.5 billion years ago, river channels spilled over the crater wall and created a lake, carrying clay minerals in from the surrounding area. Perseverance has since confirmed that Jezero once held a habitable, stable lake, delta and river system.

sections.heading: Where did the air go?
sections.body: A thicker atmosphere needs protection, and Mars lost its shield early. Mars has no global magnetic field today, but parts of its southern crust are highly magnetised — traces of a magnetic field from about 4 billion years ago. Without that protection, the solar wind can reach the upper atmosphere directly. NASA's MAVEN spacecraft, in orbit since September 2014, was the first mission devoted to understanding that upper atmosphere: how it interacts with the Sun and the solar wind, and how its gas is lost to space. That loss is the leading explanation for how a planet that once hosted rivers and lakes became the cold, dry desert seen today — and MAVEN's own mission record describes its task as determining what happened to the once-dense atmosphere of Mars.

sections.heading: A common misconception: the canals of Mars
sections.body: In the late 1800s, astronomer Percival Lowell popularised the idea that Mars was crossed by canals built by an intelligent civilisation to carry water from the polar ice caps across a drying planet. The claim rested on fine linear markings reported at the limit of what telescopes of the era could see, beginning with Giovanni Schiaparelli's 'canali'. Many astronomers were sceptical and could not see the markings; in 1909 a larger telescope at Mount Wilson showed the supposed canals were irregular natural geological features. NASA's Mariner missions in the 1960s and the Mariner 9 orbiter in 1972 then disproved canal-like features definitively: they photographed an ancient, cratered surface, and the 'canals' are now regarded as an optical illusion.

sections.heading: An open question: did anything ever live there?
sections.body: No life has been confirmed on Mars, and scientists do not expect to find living things thriving there today. The real question is whether microbial life existed long ago, when Mars was warmer and covered with water. That search is Perseverance's central task: its objectives include seeking signs of past microbial life and collecting samples of rock and soil that might preserve those signs. In 2024 the rover investigated a rock nicknamed 'Cheyava Falls' whose sample, 'Sapphire Canyon', shows signs of past water and organic material and contains potential biosignatures — clues that past life may have been present. After a year of peer review, the results were published in Nature in September 2025, with the emphasis exactly where it belongs: a potential biosignature requires more data and further study before any conclusion about life on Mars, past or present.

subjects.title: Pluto
subjects.summary: A complex icy dwarf planet with mountains, glaciers and a thin atmosphere that changes with its seasons.
subjects.description: Pluto orbits in the Kuiper Belt, a distant region populated by icy bodies. The New Horizons spacecraft revealed a surprisingly varied landscape, showing that even small, cold worlds can have rich geological histories.
facts: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Its largest moon is Charon; they orbit a shared centre of mass.
New Horizons flew past Pluto in July 2015.

subjects.title: The Moon
subjects.summary: Earth's only natural satellite: a world born from a giant collision that steadies our planet, drives the tides, and keeps the early solar system's history written in its craters.
subjects.description: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite, likely formed when a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth and the debris gathered into a new world. It orbits an average of 384,400 kilometres away, locked so that the same face always turns toward us, and its changing sunlit side gives us the lunar phases. Its gravity drives Earth's ocean tides, Apollo astronauts walked on it between 1969 and 1972, and its cratered, airless surface preserves a record of impacts that Earth has long since erased.
facts: The Moon is less than a third of Earth's width, with a radius of about 1,740 kilometres, and it orbits an average of 384,400 kilometres away — far enough that 30 Earth-sized planets could fit between us and it.
The Moon likely formed after a Mars-sized body collided with Earth several billion years ago; debris from both bodies accumulated to form our natural satellite.
The Moon rotates at exactly the rate it orbits — synchronous rotation — so the same hemisphere always faces Earth. The far side is not permanently dark: it receives just as much sunlight.
Lunar phases are changing illumination, not shadows: a full moon is the Earth-facing side fully lit by the Sun, and a new moon is that side in darkness while the far side is fully lit.
The Moon's gravity is the main driver of Earth's ocean tides, with a tide-raising effect about twice the Sun's, pulling the oceans into bulges on the sides facing toward and away from it.
With too sparse an atmosphere to slow incoming objects, the Moon has been cratered by impacts for billions of years, and the craters preserve an impact history for the whole inner solar system.
Water ice hides in permanently shadowed craters at the lunar poles, and in 2020 NASA's SOFIA observatory confirmed water molecules on the sunlit surface as well.
Between 1969 and 1972, six Apollo missions landed on the Moon and 12 astronauts walked on its surface, returning 382 kilograms of lunar rock and soil — and no one has stood on it since.

sections.heading: Born from a collision
sections.body: The leading explanation for the Moon's origin is a giant impact: several billion years ago, a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth, and debris from both bodies — flung into orbit — accumulated into the satellite we see. The newborn Moon was molten; within about 100 million years most of its global magma ocean had crystallised, with lighter rocks floating up to form the crust. The dark plains visible from Earth, the maria, came later: impact basins that flooded with lava between about 4.2 and 1.2 billion years ago. Apollo samples support the collision story — the returned rocks show the Moon formed roughly 4.5 billion years ago and preserve the chemistry of that violent beginning.

sections.heading: The Moon's grip on Earth
sections.body: The Moon's gravity is the main driver of the tides: its pull is strongest on the ocean facing it and weakest on the far side, raising two bulges that coasts pass through as Earth rotates. The Sun contributes too, but its tide-raising effect is only about half the Moon's. The same gravitational exchange that raises tides is slowly pushing the Moon away — it is receding from Earth by about an inch (a few centimetres) every year — and has locked its rotation to its orbit, which is why one face always greets us. On the Moon itself, surface gravity is one-sixth of Earth's, which is why Apollo astronauts seemed to bounce as they walked.

sections.heading: A common misconception: the 'dark side' is not dark
sections.body: The Moon's far side is often called its 'dark side', but the label misleads. Every part of the Moon takes its turn in sunlight as the Moon orbits: when we see a new moon, the far side is the one fully lit by the Sun. What the far side truly is, is unseen — synchronous rotation means it never turns toward Earth, so humanity had no image of it until spacecraft photographed it. Phases work the same way: we are not watching Earth's shadow cross the Moon (that is a lunar eclipse), just the changing angle of sunlight on the face turned toward us.

sections.heading: Still unanswered: the water, the impactor, the return
sections.body: Big questions remain open. Scientists are still mapping how much water ice the shadowed polar craters hold and where that water came from — answers that matter for any future human presence, since polar ice could support long stays. The giant-impact story also has unfinished details: the impactor's exact size, speed and composition are still being reconstructed from lunar samples and simulations. And although orbiters study the Moon constantly, no person has stood on it since Apollo 17 in 1972 — so its surface holds decades of untouched science for whoever returns.

subjects.title: Earth
subjects.summary: A dynamic planet with liquid oceans, a protective atmosphere and an extraordinary diversity of life.
subjects.description: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and, so far, the only world known to be alive. It is the only planet in our solar system with liquid water on its surface, an oxygen-rich atmosphere breathed out by life itself, and an internally generated magnetic shield — and the only one whose crust is broken into moving plates that continually rebuild its surface. A single large Moon steadies its tilt and, with it, its climate. Everything humanity knows about how planets work is anchored to this one example, which is both Earth's scientific value and its limitation. Even its name is an exception: every other planet carries the name of a Greek or Roman god; 'Earth' simply means 'the ground.'
facts: Earth is the only planet in our solar system with liquid water on its surface. Its global ocean covers about 71% of the surface, averages about 3.6 kilometres deep, and holds 97% of all Earth's water.
Earth is the biggest of the four rocky terrestrial planets and the fifth largest planet overall, with an equatorial diameter of 12,756 kilometres.
Earth orbits exactly one astronomical unit — about 150 million kilometres — from the Sun, by definition; sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us.
Earth spins once every 23.9 hours and takes 365.25 days to orbit the Sun. The extra quarter-day is why our calendar adds a leap day every four years.
Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, when gravity pulled swirling gas and dust together; life began in its vast oceans about 3.8 billion years ago.

The atmosphere is 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% other gases. It shields the surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation, and most incoming meteoroids burn up in it as meteors before they can strike.
Earth's rapid rotation and molten nickel-iron core generate a magnetic field. The geologic record shows its polarity flips on average about every 300,000 years — but at very irregular intervals.

Earth is the only body in the solar system known to show plate tectonics in action: its outer layer is broken into a dozen or more plates moving between less than 1 and more than 15 centimetres a year, and more than 80% of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes occur along their boundaries.

sections.heading: A planet built in layers
sections.body: Slice Earth open and it is not solid rock all the way down. At the centre sits an inner core: a solid sphere of iron and nickel about 1,221 kilometres in radius, where the temperature reaches about 5,400 °C — as hot as the Sun's surface. Around it churns a liquid outer core of iron and nickel some 2,300 kilometres thick; Earth's rotation in that molten metal is what generates the planet's magnetic field, the shield that deflects the solar wind and paints the aurorae at the poles. Above the core lies the mantle, roughly 2,900 kilometres of hot, slowly flowing rock that NASA compares to caramel, and finally the crust — about 30 kilometres thick under the continents, but only about 5 kilometres thick under the oceans. Everything we have ever directly sampled is that thin outer skin.

sections.heading: The restless surface
sections.body: The crust and upper mantle are not one shell but a mosaic — a dozen or more rigid plates riding on hotter, softer rock beneath, drifting between less than 1 and more than 15 centimetres a year. At mid-ocean ridges the plates pull apart and new seafloor is born; at subduction zones an old, cold plate sinks back into the interior and is recycled. That conveyor is why the oldest seafloor is only about 180 million years old while the oldest known continental rock, in Australia, dates back about 4.3 billion years — the oceans keep renewing their floors while continents mostly survive. The present continents are fragments of a supercontinent, Pangaea, that broke up about 225 million years ago. And the process is not gentle: more than 80% of earthquakes and volcanoes happen along the plate boundaries. Earth is, as far as anyone has found, the only planet where this is happening.

sections.heading: A common misconception: summer is not Earth moving closer to the Sun
sections.body: It feels obvious: summer is hot, so Earth must be nearer the Sun. NASA calls the idea out directly — it is incorrect. Earth's orbit is slightly lopsided, but the timing gives it away: Earth is closest to the Sun (perihelion, about 91.4 million miles) in January and farthest (aphelion, about 94.5 million miles) in July — so the Northern Hemisphere has winter at closest approach and summer at the farthest point, and the roughly 3-million-mile difference is too small, relative to the whole distance, to drive the weather. The real cause is tilt. Earth's axis leans 23.4 degrees, so as the planet orbits, each hemisphere takes its turn leaning toward the Sun and receiving its rays more directly — summer where you lean in, winter where you lean away, and opposite seasons in the two hemispheres. The same tilt is thought to be a souvenir of the collision with a body called Theia early in Earth's history — the impact that most scientists believe blasted out the rubble that became our Moon.

sections.heading: An open question: how did a rocky planet become a living one?
sections.body: Earth is the only place in the universe where life is known to exist, and we still cannot say exactly how it started. NASA's summary is deliberately modest: Earth's oceans provided a convenient place for life to begin about 3.8 billion years ago. The steps from ocean chemistry to the first living cell — which molecules came first, where exactly it happened, and how likely it is anywhere else — remain unresolved, and they matter far beyond Earth: the answer shapes how scientists judge the odds of life on ocean worlds and exoplanets. Some of Earth's other basics are just as unsettled. We know the magnetic field has reversed many times, at irregular intervals averaging about 300,000 years — and that a reversal is very unlikely in the next thousand years — but there is no way to schedule the next one. Our home planet is the best-studied world there is, and parts of its own story are still open.

subjects.title: Dinosaurs
subjects.summary: A remarkable group of animals that dominated many land ecosystems for over 160 million years.
subjects.description: Dinosaurs evolved into an astonishing range of forms during the Mesozoic Era. Fossils, geological context and modern analytical methods help scientists reconstruct how they lived and interacted with changing environments.
facts: Birds are living dinosaurs, descended from theropod dinosaurs.
Non-avian dinosaurs disappeared about 66 million years ago.
Fossils provide evidence, but many behavioural details remain open to research.

subjects.title: Evolution
subjects.summary: The change in inherited characteristics of populations across generations, shaping the diversity of life.
subjects.description: Evolution is descent with inherited modification: populations change across generations, and given deep time, that process connects every living thing to shared ancestors. It is the unifying framework of biology, supported independently by fossils, comparative anatomy, biogeography and DNA — and observable in action today, from drug-resistant bacteria to fish adapting to polluted rivers. Its mechanisms are unspectacular: variation, inheritance, and more offspring than the environment can support. Compounded over billions of years, their product is the entire diversity of life. Humans are part of that story, not its destination — one twig on an immense tree, close cousins to chimpanzees and bonobos, and distant ones to oak trees and whales.
facts: Evolution is descent with inherited modification: changes in the inherited traits of populations across generations. Individuals do not evolve during their own lifetimes — populations do.

All life on Earth shares a common ancestor, just as cousins share a grandmother. Humans and oak trees, hummingbirds and whales, are distant relatives, connected through the fossil record and the living world.

Natural selection needs only three ingredients: variation in traits, differential reproduction (not every individual gets to reproduce equally), and heredity. Given those, evolution by natural selection follows automatically.

Selection is not the only mechanism. Mutation generates new variation, gene flow moves it between populations, and genetic drift changes trait frequencies purely by chance — an effect strongest in small populations but present in all of them.

Humans, chimpanzees and bonobos descend from a single ancestor species that lived six or seven million years ago. Humans and chimps share 98.8% of their DNA — and the remaining 1.2% of roughly three billion base pairs still amounts to about 35 million differences.

Evolution can be fast enough to watch. Within the past 50 years, scientists have documented microbes evolving resistance to new drugs, a fish species evolving resistance to toxins dumped in the Hudson River, and squirrels shifting their breeding times as the climate warms.

Humans are still evolving. Technology has changed which challenges matter — dense populations favour gene versions that protect against epidemic disease, for instance — and documented recent human adaptations include lactose tolerance persisting into adulthood and traits for thriving at high altitude.

Evolution has no ladder and no goal. It produces a branching tree, not progress toward perfection: some lineages, like certain mosses, fungi, sharks and opossums, have changed little physically over vast spans of time.

sections.heading: Three ingredients, and change follows
sections.body: Natural selection sounds grand, but UC Berkeley's classic example is a population of beetles. Some are green, some brown. Birds spot the green ones against the bark more easily, so brown beetles survive to reproduce more often. The trait is heritable, so the next generation is browner — and repeated over generations, the population changes. That is the whole engine: variation, differential reproduction, heredity. Two refinements matter. First, the variation itself arises by random mutation, but selection is not random — it systematically favours variants that leave more offspring, which is how intricate adaptations like the fit between a flower and its pollinator arise without any designer or foresight. Second, 'fitness' is not strength or health: it simply means getting more of your genes into the next generation. A small, drab organism that reproduces well is fitter, in the only sense evolution counts, than a magnificent one that leaves no offspring. And selection has no intentions — it cannot give a population what it 'needs'; if the useful variation is not there, the population may simply die out.

sections.heading: Independent evidence, one tree
sections.body: Evolution would be a weak idea if it rested on one kind of clue. Instead, separate fields keep arriving at the same family tree. The fossil record documents change over time directly, including fossils with transitional features — exactly what the theory predicts should sometimes be preserved, given how rarely fossilisation happens — and detailed sequences such as whales evolving gradually from land-dwelling mammal ancestors. Comparative anatomy finds the same nested pattern: groups within groups, sharing inherited structures. Genetics then tests that tree with entirely different data, and it holds: the American Museum of Natural History notes that humans and chimps have many identical genes, often used at different levels — the same brain genes, for example, expressed in different amounts — a pattern of shared inheritance with modification, not separate creation. For our own lineage, the Smithsonian's Human Origins Program organises the evidence the same way: fossil species, stone tools, ancient footprints, and ancient DNA, which has even shown that modern humans interbred with Neanderthals. Fossils predicted the relationships; DNA, unknown to Darwin, confirmed them.

sections.heading: Two common misconceptions: “just a theory” and “humans evolved from chimps”
sections.body: The first is a confusion between two meanings of one word. In everyday speech, a theory is a hunch. In science, a theory is a broad explanation that has been strongly supported by many different lines of evidence — gravity and germs are 'theories' in exactly this sense. Evolutionary theory is not a guess awaiting proof; it is the framework that explains observations from antibiotic resistance to the match between flowers and their pollinators, and that makes accurate predictions, such as the finding that treating HIV with drug cocktails slows the virus's evolution. The second misconception gets the family tree wrong. Humans did not evolve from chimpanzees, and chimpanzees did not evolve from humans: both descend from a single ancestor species that lived six or seven million years ago, and each lineage has been evolving ever since. That is why the right picture is not a ladder with apes below and humans on top, but a branching tree — chimps are our cousins, not our grandparents, and we are one twig among millions.

sections.heading: An open question: what evolution does not claim to explain
sections.body: It is worth being precise about the boundary of the theory, because UC Berkeley's evolution resource states it plainly: evolutionary theory is mostly not about the origin of life. It deals with how life changed after it began — how one population branched into the diversity we see. How the first self-replicating chemistry became the first cell is a separate, genuinely open research problem (one this library's Earth guide flags as well), and uncertainty there is not evidence against evolution, any more than not knowing the Sun's exact birth cloud counts against astronomy. Within evolution itself, scientists debate plenty — but the debates are about how, not whether: how fast change happens in different lineages, the relative weight of selection versus drift, exactly where each fossil species sits on our own branch of the tree. Those arguments continue because new fossils and new genomes keep arriving to argue with. 'We do not know everything' is the normal condition of a living science, not a crack in this one.

sources.title: Comparing Chimp, Bonobo and Human DNA

subjects.title: Supernovae
subjects.eyebrow: When stars reach a turning point
subjects.summary: Powerful stellar explosions that can briefly outshine entire galaxies and distribute elements into space.
subjects.description: A supernova can occur when a massive star's core collapses or when a white dwarf undergoes a runaway thermonuclear explosion. These events shape galaxies and disperse elements; some leave neutron stars or black holes.
facts: Different physical mechanisms produce different types of supernovae.
Supernova remnants enrich the interstellar medium.
A supernova does not always leave a black hole.

subjects.title: Earth's Oceans
subjects.summary: A connected global ocean system that regulates climate and supports an immense diversity of life.
subjects.description: The oceans store and move heat, shape weather, and support diverse ecosystems — including deep-sea communities at hydrothermal vents that thrive without sunlight.
facts: The ocean is central to Earth's climate system.
Deep-sea ecosystems can thrive without sunlight, including near hydrothermal vents.
Ocean science ranges from surface weather and currents to deep-sea ecosystems that thrive without sunlight near hydrothermal vents.

sources.title: How does the ocean affect climate and weather on land?

subjects.title: The Universe
subjects.summary: Space, time, matter and energy on the largest scales—and the questions that remain unanswered.
subjects.description: Modern cosmology describes a universe that has expanded and cooled from an early hot, dense state. Observations of galaxies and cosmic background radiation have transformed our understanding, while dark matter, dark energy and the earliest moments remain active research topics.
facts: The observable universe is limited by the speed of light and cosmic expansion.
The Big Bang model describes the universe's early hot, dense evolution.
The full universe may extend beyond the region we can observe.

subjects.title: Gravity
subjects.summary: The weakest of the fundamental forces, yet the one that builds stars, steers planets, bends light and shapes the cosmos — described first by Newton, then reimagined by Einstein as the curvature of spacetime itself.
subjects.description: Gravity is the attraction between anything with mass, and it runs the universe at large scales. Newton's law of universal gravitation (1687) made it predictable: pull grows with mass and fades with the square of distance. Einstein's general relativity (1915) went deeper, describing gravity not as a force but as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy — a picture confirmed by bending starlight, Mercury's orbit, and the gravitational waves LIGO detected in 2015. Gravity gathers gas into stars and galaxies, holds planets in orbit, raises the tides — and still refuses to fit into quantum physics, leaving it the most familiar and least finished force in science.
facts: Anything that has mass has gravity: the more mass an object has, the stronger its pull, and the pull weakens as distance grows.

Newton's law (1687) quantifies the attraction: it grows with both masses and falls with the square of the distance — which is why the nearby Moon raises about twice the Sun's tide despite the Sun's far greater mass.
You pull on Earth with exactly the same force Earth pulls on you; Earth's enormous mass is why its response to your pull is far too small to notice.
Einstein's general relativity describes gravity not as a force but as a curve in space that wraps around an object such as a star or planet, pulling nearby objects — even light — into the curve.

Gravity is by far the weakest of the four fundamental interactions, yet with infinite range and no cancellation it is the most significant force between objects at large scales, determining the motion of planets, stars, galaxies, and even light.
Changes in gravity travel at the speed of light: move a mass, and the resulting ripples in spacetime spread outward no faster than light does.

In 2015, LIGO detected those ripples directly — gravitational waves from two black holes of about 29 and 36 solar masses that collided 1.3 billion years ago, converting about 3 solar masses into the waves themselves.

Gravity is not the same everywhere on Earth: it is slightly stronger over places with more mass underground, and NASA's GRACE twin spacecraft mapped those variations, revealing changes in sea level and in Earth's crust after earthquakes.

sections.heading: Newton's law, Einstein's geometry
sections.body: Newton's Principia (1687) gave gravity a formula: attraction proportional to the product of the masses, inversely proportional to the square of the distance. It was powerful enough that in 1846 astronomers used it to predict Neptune's position from wobbles in Uranus's orbit — and found the planet within a day. But one number refused to fit: Mercury's orbit precesses by about 43 arcseconds per century more than Newton allows. Einstein's general relativity (1915) explained it exactly, by replacing force with geometry — mass curves spacetime, and objects follow the curves. Its prediction that starlight bends near the Sun was confirmed in the eclipse expeditions of 1919. For most everyday calculations Newton's law remains accurate enough, which is why spacecraft are still largely navigated with it.

sections.heading: The architect of structure
sections.body: Gravity built everything large. In the early universe it pulled the original gas together until it coalesced into stars, and stars into galaxies; today it holds planets in orbit around the Sun, the Moon in orbit around Earth, and stars in their galactic rounds. It is also the force we feel most directly: it holds down the atmosphere, keeps the oceans in their basins, gives us weight — and, through the Moon's pull, raises the tides twice a day. Black holes are its extreme case, packing so much mass into so little volume that their gravity keeps even light from escaping; the waves LIGO heard in 2015 were the sound of two such objects merging, a century after Einstein predicted ripples in spacetime.

sections.heading: A common misconception: there is no 'zero gravity' in orbit
sections.body: Astronauts float in orbit not because gravity has switched off — at the space station's altitude it is nearly as strong as on the ground — but because they and their spacecraft are falling together around Earth, in continuous free fall that never lands. 'Zero gravity' is a misnomer for that shared falling. Two other confusions are worth clearing up: gravity needs no air or medium to work through (it acts across the vacuum of space), and it is not magnetism — it relates only to mass, pulling everything with mass, charged or not.

sections.heading: Still unanswered: gravity and the quantum world
sections.body: For all its success, gravity is unfinished. General relativity describes the very large superbly and quantum mechanics describes the very small superbly, but the two frameworks still do not fit together, and scientists are working to develop a theory of quantum gravity that unites gravity with the other three fundamental interactions in one mathematical framework. Until that exists, the earliest moments of the universe and the interiors of black holes — where both theories must apply at once — stay partly out of reach. The weakest force remains the deepest puzzle.

sources.title: LIGO Opens New Window on the Universe with Observation of Gravitational Waves from Colliding Black Holes
Ask Us — Gravity
sources.publisher: NASA Cosmicopia, Goddard Space Flight Center

subjects.title: Stars
subjects.summary: Vast spheres of hot plasma whose life cycles help shape the chemistry and structure of the universe.
subjects.description: Stars form from collapsing clouds of gas and dust. Their mass strongly influences how they shine, how long they live, and what remains after their fuel is exhausted.
facts: A star's mass is one of the main factors determining its life cycle.
Fusion in stellar interiors builds many elements found throughout the universe.
Most stars form as members of star clusters created by the collapse of dense clumps of gas and dust.

subjects.title: Galaxies
subjects.summary: Vast gravitationally bound systems of stars, gas, dust and dark matter, shaped across cosmic time.
subjects.description: Galaxies come in a range of forms, from spiral and elliptical systems to irregular galaxies. They grow and change through star formation, interactions and mergers. By observing galaxies at different distances, astronomers also study how the universe has evolved.
facts: Galaxies contain stars, interstellar gas and dust, and dark matter.
Galaxy shapes and activity change over billions of years.
The Milky Way and Andromeda may collide and merge in the distant future, but recent Hubble and Gaia simulations put the chance of a collision within the next 10 billion years at roughly 50-50.

sources.title: Apocalypse When? Hubble Casts Doubt on Certainty of Galactic Collision

subjects.title: Exoplanets
subjects.summary: Planets orbiting stars beyond our Sun, spanning an astonishing range of sizes, orbits and environments.
subjects.description: Astronomers have confirmed thousands of exoplanets using methods such as transits and radial velocity. Some orbit close to their stars; others travel in cold, distant orbits. Finding a planet does not by itself mean it hosts life, but studying these worlds helps scientists understand how planetary systems form and how common Earth-like conditions might be.
facts: A transit occurs when a planet passes in front of its star from our viewpoint.
The habitable zone is defined by conditions where liquid water could exist on a suitable planet's surface, not by proof of life.
Atmospheric observations can help researchers investigate exoplanet chemistry.

subjects.title: Climate Change
subjects.summary: Long-term shifts in temperatures and weather patterns, with modern global warming driven primarily by human activities.
subjects.description: Climate change is the long-term shift in Earth's climate now under way — and it differs from the slow natural swings of the ice ages in both speed and cause. The warming is measured by many independent instruments at once, and the IPCC assesses that human activities, principally greenhouse-gas emissions, have unequivocally caused it. The evidence is not a single graph: thermometers and satellites, ice cores and tree rings, tide gauges and ocean robots all record a planet accumulating heat — warming air and land, heating oceans, melting ice and raising seas. How much more warming this century brings is not fixed by physics alone; it depends substantially on emissions choices made in the coming decades.
facts: The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report states it without hedging: human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming. Global surface temperature in 2011–2020 reached 1.1 °C above the 1850–1900 average.
2024 was the warmest year since global records began in 1850 — about 1.46 °C above the pre-industrial average — and the ten warmest years on record have all occurred in the last decade, 2015–2024.
The warming has accelerated: about 0.06 °C per decade since 1850, but 0.20 °C per decade since 1975. It has been nearly five decades since Earth last had a cooler-than-average year.

Atmospheric carbon dioxide reached 410 parts per million in 2019 — higher than at any time in at least 2 million years. Methane and nitrous oxide concentrations were higher than at any time in at least 800,000 years.

Of the warming between 1850–1900 and 2010–2019, the IPCC's best estimate of the human-caused share is 1.07 °C. Natural drivers — the Sun and volcanoes — changed global temperature by only about −0.1 to +0.1 °C over the same period.

The ocean stores about 90% of the extra energy trapped in the Earth system. Its top 100 metres have warmed by about 0.33 °C since 1969, and the acidity of surface ocean water has increased by about 30% since the Industrial Revolution.

The ice is going. Between 1993 and 2019, Greenland lost an average of about 279 billion tonnes of ice per year and Antarctica about 148 billion tonnes per year; glaciers are retreating almost everywhere, and Arctic sea ice has declined rapidly in both extent and thickness.

Global mean sea level rose about 20 centimetres between 1901 and 2018, and the rate has climbed — from about 1.3 millimetres a year early last century to 3.7 millimetres a year during 2006–2018 — driven by melting land ice and by seawater expanding as it warms.

sections.heading: Not one graph — a planet full of instruments
sections.body: The case for a warming planet does not rest on any single measurement. Weather stations and satellites track surface temperature, and multiple independent research groups analysing the data separately all show a similar upward trend. The oceans confirm it independently: a global fleet of buoys, ships and drifting robots measures rising heat content, and about 90% of the extra energy accumulating in the Earth system is stored there. Satellites weighing the ice sheets through their gravity (NASA's GRACE missions) watch Greenland and Antarctica lose mass; tide gauges running for over a century, and radar altimeters in orbit since the 1990s, watch sea level climb. And for the centuries before instruments, ice cores, tree rings, ocean sediments and coral reefs preserve a natural archive — one that shows today's warming standing out sharply from the past. Different methods, different teams, different physics: the same direction.

sections.heading: Why the evidence points at greenhouse gases
sections.body: The basic mechanism is old, settled physics: scientists demonstrated the heat-trapping nature of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in the mid-19th century. Greenhouse gases let Earth absorb more energy from the Sun than it radiates back to space, and the planet warms until the balance is restored. Attribution studies then ask what actually did it. The IPCC's accounting for 1850–1900 to 2010–2019 finds greenhouse gases alone contributed between 1.0 and 2.0 °C of warming, partly masked by a cooling effect from human aerosol pollution, while natural drivers — changes in the Sun and volcanic eruptions — contributed essentially nothing, between −0.1 and +0.1 °C. The fingerprint also shows in the speed of the carbon itself: carbon dioxide from human activities is increasing about 250 times faster than it did from natural sources after the last Ice Age.

sections.heading: A common misconception: “the climate changed naturally before, so this is natural too”
sections.body: The first half is true. In just the last 800,000 years Earth has swung through eight cycles of ice ages and warmer periods, driven by very small variations in Earth's orbit that change the sunlight the planet receives — and nobody disputes that climate can change on its own. What the argument misses is rate and cause. Paleoclimate records show the current warming is occurring roughly ten times faster than the average rate of warming as Earth recovered from an ice age, and the IPCC finds global surface temperature has risen faster since 1970 than in any other 50-year period in at least 2,000 years. Meanwhile the natural drivers that explain past changes have been measured for this period and come out near zero — they cannot account for what is observed, while human greenhouse-gas emissions can. If anything, the ancient evidence strengthens the conclusion: ice cores show that Earth's climate responds directly to greenhouse-gas levels. When the gases moved slowly, climate moved slowly. Now the gases are moving fast.

sections.heading: An open question: how much more — and how fast can the ice go?
sections.body: The largest unknown in climate change is not the physics but us. The IPCC finds that continued emissions lead to increasing warming, with the best estimate reaching 1.5 °C in the near term in the scenarios it assessed — and that every increment of warming intensifies multiple hazards at once. Beyond that, how much warmer the planet gets depends mainly on how much carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases are emitted in coming decades: a choice, not a constant. A second genuine unknown is the ice sheets. Some sea-level rise is already locked in — NOAA's interagency assessment concludes global mean sea level will rise at least about 0.3 metres above 2000 levels by 2100 even on the lowest emissions pathway — but the upper end depends on whether the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets melt in a steady, predictable way or reach a tipping point and collapse rapidly. That difference is worth metres of sea level over the following century, and narrowing it down is one of the most consequential open problems in Earth science.

sources.title: Climate Change 2023: Synthesis Report — Summary for Policymakers

subjects.title: Whales
subjects.summary: Marine mammals with complex social lives, remarkable adaptations and important roles in ocean ecosystems.
subjects.description: Whales are mammals that breathe air, give birth to live young and nurse them with milk. Baleen whales filter-feed, while toothed whales use teeth and, in many species, echolocation. Their evolution from land-dwelling ancestors is documented by fossils, and modern research explores their communication, migration and conservation.
facts: Whales must surface to breathe air, even though they live in water.
Baleen and toothed whales use different feeding strategies.
Many whale populations were heavily reduced by commercial whaling; recovery varies by species and region.

subjects.title: Human Origins
subjects.summary: The evidence-based study of how our species emerged within a diverse family tree of ancient humans.
subjects.description: Human origins research brings together fossils, archaeology, genetics and comparisons with other primates. Human evolution was not a straight line: multiple hominin species existed, spread, adapted and sometimes interbred. New discoveries and methods continue to refine this picture.
facts: Modern humans, Homo sapiens, evolved in Africa.
More than 20 hominin species are now known, and new fossil discoveries keep rearranging the human family tree.
Genetic evidence shows that some people today carry ancestry from other ancient human groups.

sources.title: Human Evolution Evidence
sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History

subjects.title: Language
subjects.summary: The shared system of sounds, signs and marks that lets humans share thoughts — more than 7,000 languages strong, learned effortlessly in childhood, and written down only in the last few thousand years.
subjects.description: Language is a set of shared rules that lets people express ideas in a meaningful way — spoken aloud, signed with the hands, or written in marks. Every human community has one, and children acquire theirs in the first years of life simply by being surrounded by it. More than 7,000 languages are in use today, from the 23 that carry more than half of humanity to thousands spoken by small communities, roughly 40% of them endangered. Speech itself is ancient and leaves no direct record; writing is the recent invention, barely 5,000 years old, that let language outlive its speakers.
facts: More than 7,000 languages are in use around the world today, and the count is always in flux as languages are documented, change, merge, or fall silent.
Speakers are spread very unevenly: just 23 languages account for more than half of the world's population.
Roughly 40% of the world's languages are endangered, often with fewer than 1,000 users remaining.
Sign languages are fully fledged natural languages, structurally distinct from spoken languages: more than 70 million deaf people use more than 300 of them.
The first three years of life are the most intensive period for acquiring speech and language, and there appear to be critical periods when the brain is best able to absorb it.
By six months of age, most babies already recognise the basic sounds of their native language, and one or two first words typically follow by the first birthday.

The earliest known writing system was Sumerian cuneiform, traced to the end of the 4th millennium BCE; its earliest records are pictographic tablets from Uruk listing commodities, numerals and personal names.
Writing grew out of bookkeeping: clay tokens used to count goods as early as about 8000 BCE evolved, via marked clay envelopes, into inscribed clay tablets — the first writing.

sections.heading: How children learn a language
sections.body: Children do not learn their first language from lessons. The first three years of life are the most intensive period for acquiring speech and language, and the skills develop best in a world rich with sounds and consistent exposure to the speech of others. The timetable is remarkably regular: by six months most babies recognise the basic sounds of their native language; one or two words arrive around the first birthday; two-word phrases follow, then sentences, and by four or five most children use adult grammar. There appear to be critical periods when the brain is best able to absorb language — if they pass without exposure, learning becomes much harder. And language is not only speech: it is a set of shared rules that may be expressed verbally, by writing, by signing, or by other gestures.

sections.heading: Writing: language that outlives its speakers
sections.body: Spoken language is ancient; writing is young. The earliest known writing system was Sumerian cuneiform, emerging around the end of the 4th millennium BCE in southern Mesopotamia. Its roots were practical: small clay tokens used to count grain, sheep and cattle — some dating to about 8000 BCE — were sealed in clay envelopes, the envelopes were marked with the tokens' shapes, and eventually the marks alone, pressed into clay with a stylus, became the record. The earliest tablets from Uruk are ledgers: lists of commodities with drawings, numerals and personal names. Over time signs came to stand for sounds as well as things, and cuneiform spread across cultures and languages for three millennia. Other societies devised their own systems with independent indigenous origins — Egyptian hieroglyphs and Chinese characters among them — each turning fleeting speech into something that could cross centuries.

sections.heading: A common misconception: sign language is one universal code of gestures
sections.body: There is no single sign language. More than 300 distinct sign languages are in use, each a fully fledged natural language, structurally distinct from the spoken languages around it — British and American sign languages, for example, are mutually unintelligible despite sharing English as a neighbour. Sign languages have their own grammar, vocabulary and regional dialects, and they evolve naturally within their communities, exactly as spoken languages do. The one partial exception proves the rule: International Sign, used at conferences and Deaf sporting events, is a simplified contact system — a pidgin, not a full language. The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recognises sign languages as equal in status to spoken languages.

sections.heading: Still unanswered: where did language itself come from?
sections.body: Writing's birth is documented in clay; speech leaves no fossils. When language emerged — whether gradually over hundreds of thousands of years or in a more sudden leap — and what exactly changed in the human brain and vocal tract to make it possible, remains one of science's great open questions. Researchers attack it from many sides: the fossil record of our ancestors, the genetics of speech and hearing, the study of how children acquire language so effortlessly, and comparisons with how other animals communicate. A related question is more urgent than academic: with roughly 40% of today's languages endangered, much of humanity's linguistic diversity — and the knowledge carried only in those languages — could vanish within generations unless communities and linguists document and revive them.

sources.title: How many languages are there in the world?
Speech and Language Developmental Milestones
sources.publisher: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

subjects.title: Ancient Civilizations
subjects.summary: The diverse societies that developed cities, states, writing systems, trade networks and lasting cultural traditions.
subjects.description: Ancient civilizations emerged in different places under different conditions. Archaeology, written records, oral histories and environmental evidence help reconstruct how people organized communities, exchanged goods, governed, worshipped and adapted. No single civilization represents the whole human story.
facts: Complex societies developed independently in several world regions.
Writing appeared in different forms and contexts rather than through one universal path.
Archaeological interpretations can change as new evidence is discovered.

subjects.title: The Moon Landing
subjects.eyebrow: Humanity's first step on another world
subjects.summary: On 20 July 1969, Apollo 11 put the first humans on the Moon — the end of an eight-year race, watched by an estimated 650 million people, and the first of six landings that brought back 382 kilograms of another world.
subjects.description: The Moon landing was the moment humanity first stood on another world. Apollo 11 launched on 16 July 1969, and four days later Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle in the Sea of Tranquility while Michael Collins orbited above in Columbia. They spent 21 hours 36 minutes on the surface, gathered samples, deployed experiments — including a laser reflector still in use today — and splashed down safely on 24 July. Five more landings followed by 1972, and no one has stood on the Moon since. The hardware they left behind has since been photographed from lunar orbit, and the rocks they brought back are still being studied.
facts: Apollo 11's objective was a national goal set by President John F. Kennedy on 25 May 1961: a crewed lunar landing and safe return to Earth — achieved eight years later.

Apollo 11 launched from Cape Kennedy on 16 July 1969 carrying Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin, and flew a free-return trajectory that could bring it home without an engine firing until lunar orbit insertion.
Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility on 20 July 1969, partially piloted manually by Armstrong, who flew past a crater in the final seconds — touching down about four miles past the predicted point.
Armstrong stepped onto the surface about 109 hours 42 minutes into the flight, Aldrin followed about 20 minutes later, and an estimated 650 million people watched the televised step.
The two astronauts spent 21 hours 36 minutes on the surface, including a moonwalk of more than two and a half hours, ranging up to 300 feet from Eagle and gathering lunar samples.
Apollo 11 splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on 24 July 1969, 13 miles from the recovery ship USS Hornet, after a flight of 8 days, 3 hours and 18 minutes covering 953,054 miles.
Apollo 11 was the first of six successful landings: between 1969 and 1972, 12 astronauts walked on the Moon and returned 382 kilograms of lunar rock and soil.

The landing sites are still visible and measurable: in 2009 the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed the descent stages and astronaut footpaths, and the laser reflector Apollo 11 left behind is still ranged by telescopes on Earth.

sections.heading: The race to the Moon
sections.body: Apollo 11 was the end of a race, not the start of one. In May 1961, weeks after Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, President Kennedy set the United States a goal that sounded impossible: land a person on the Moon and return them safely before the decade was out. The Apollo program that answered him grew into one of the largest peacetime undertakings in history, employing some 400,000 people at its peak and costing roughly $257 billion in 2020 dollars. Apollo 11 flew a free-return trajectory — a path that would loop around the Moon and bring the crew home even if the main engine failed — and it was the last Apollo mission to do so. When Eagle separated from Columbia on 20 July, the goal was eight years old, and the whole world was watching.

sections.heading: Eight days in July
sections.body: Apollo 11 launched at 9:32 a.m. EDT on 16 July 1969. After a translunar burn, the crew coasted for three days, entered lunar orbit on 19 July, and on 20 July Armstrong and Aldrin climbed into Eagle and began their descent. The final minutes were the tensest of the mission: Armstrong took partial manual control, flew past a boulder-strewn crater, and landed with the descent running 40 seconds longer than planned. The first moonwalk had been scheduled after a four-hour rest; instead, Armstrong stepped out about four hours after landing, deployed the television camera, and spoke the line an estimated 650 million people heard live. The crew deployed experiments, gathered samples, slept seven hours on the surface, then lifted off to dock with Collins and fly home — splashing down in the Pacific on 24 July, 13 miles from the USS Hornet.

sections.heading: A common misconception: it was faked in a studio
sections.body: No historical event of the 20th century has attracted more conspiracy theories — and few are so thoroughly checkable. The hardware is still there: in July 2009, NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed five of the six landing sites, showing the lunar module descent stages, the experiment packages, and the faint trails of astronaut footprints between them; the sixth site followed weeks later. The science is still running: the panel of 100 mirrors Apollo 11 left behind — with two more from Apollos 14 and 15 — is still ranged by lasers from telescopes on Earth, measuring the Earth–Moon distance precisely enough to reveal the Moon's liquid core and test general relativity. And the evidence is in laboratories: 382 kilograms of lunar rock and soil, returned by six crews, have been studied by scientists in many countries for over fifty years.

sections.heading: Still unanswered: why we stopped, and what comes next
sections.body: The strangest fact about the Moon landings may be that they ended. Apollo 17 left the surface in December 1972, and no human has stood on the Moon since — the program was cancelled as its cost and political urgency faded, not because the science was finished. The unfinished work is still there: Apollo samples continue to yield discoveries as new instruments examine them, and the laser reflectors are now joined by proposals for a new generation of arrays that could probe dark matter and dark energy. The Moon itself has not changed — the footprints, the descent stages and the mirrors sit exactly where they were left, in a world with no wind to erase them. The open question is not whether we can go back, but when, and what we will do differently when we do.

sources.title: LROC's first look at the Apollo landing sites

subjects.title: Mathematics
subjects.summary: A broad field for studying patterns, structures, quantities and change through precise reasoning.
subjects.description: Mathematics includes number, geometry, algebra, probability, statistics and many other fields. It develops through definitions, logical arguments and proof, and it also provides tools for describing natural phenomena, building technology and reasoning about uncertainty. Mathematical traditions grew across many cultures and eras.
facts: A mathematical proof explains why a statement follows from accepted assumptions.
Probability and statistics help describe uncertainty and evidence.
Mathematics is both an abstract discipline and a practical language used across science and engineering.

subjects.title: Artificial Intelligence
subjects.summary: Methods for building computer systems that perform tasks associated with perception, prediction, language and decision-making.
subjects.description: Artificial intelligence is a broad family of techniques rather than one single technology. Modern systems may use machine learning, neural networks, search, planning or rule-based methods. Their capabilities and limitations depend on their design, training data, evaluation and context; fluent output alone is not proof that a system is correct or understands a subject as a person does.
facts: Machine learning systems infer patterns from data or experience rather than relying only on hand-written rules.
AI systems can produce confident but incorrect outputs, so important claims need verification.
Responsible AI work includes evaluating reliability, privacy, bias, safety and real-world effects.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence
sources.publisher: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence

subjects.title: Baobab
subjects.summary: Nine species of long-lived trees with barrel-like trunks that store water, native to Madagascar, Africa and Australia.
subjects.description: Baobabs are deciduous trees of the genus Adansonia, known for their barrel-like trunks and extraordinary longevity. An Arabian legend says the devil plucked up the baobab, thrust its branches into the earth, and left its roots in the air — the tree's shape really does look upside down. The African baobab is called the Tree of Life: local peoples use its edible leaves and fruit, its bark fibre for rope and cloth, and its hollow trunks as water reserves and shelter.
facts: There are nine baobab species: seven are endemic to Madagascar, one is native to mainland Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, and one to northwestern Australia.
The African baobab boasts the oldest known angiosperm tree: carbon-14 dating places the age of a specimen in Namibia at about 1,275 years.
The African baobab's water-storing trunk may reach a diameter of 9 meters (30 feet) and a height of 18 meters (59 feet).

subjects.title: Coast Redwood
subjects.summary: Sequoia sempervirens, the world's tallest trees, living for two millennia in a narrow fog-fed coastal band.
subjects.description: The coast redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) is an evergreen conifer of the cypress family, closely related to the giant sequoia. Its Latin name means “always green, flourishing”. Redwoods survive millennia with 12-inch-thick fire-resistant bark, tannins that repel insects and disease, and shallow roots that intertwine with neighbours for stability — yet they have no taproot at all.
facts: A coast redwood's straight, reddish-brown trunk reaches over 350 feet, making it the tallest tree in the world; a mature tree can exceed 20 feet in diameter at ground level.
Redwood forests grow natively in a narrow band along the Pacific Coast, from central California to southern Oregon, depending on a maritime climate of stable temperature, moisture and fog.
Old-growth redwood forest historically covered 2 million acres in California; just 4% of the original old-growth forest remains today, much of it in Redwood National and State Parks.

subjects.title: Mango Tree
subjects.eyebrow: The king of fruits, from South Asia
subjects.summary: Mangifera indica, a long-lived tropical tree cultivated for thousands of years, and the national tree of Bangladesh.
subjects.description: The mango tree (Mangifera indica) produces one of the most celebrated tropical fruits — and, surprisingly, belongs to the cashew family, notorious for embracing a number of highly poisonous plants. Native to southern Asia, it has been cultivated, praised and even revered in its homeland since ancient times, and Buddhist monks are believed to have carried it on voyages to Malaya and eastern Asia in the 4th and 5th centuries BCE.
facts: A mango tree grows 30 to 100 feet high with a broad canopy up to 125 feet wide; the tree is long-lived, some specimens being known to be 300 years old and still fruiting.
The cultivated mango originated in the Indo-Burma region, and it has been grown in India for the last 6,000 years.
The mango is the national fruit of India, Pakistan and the Philippines, and the mango tree is the national tree of Bangladesh.

sources.title: Mango
sources.publisher: Purdue University — Fruits of Warm Climates

subjects.title: Bonsai
subjects.eyebrow: A whole tree, in a tray
subjects.summary: The art of training ordinary trees into miniature living sculptures in containers, from China to Japan and the world.
subjects.description: Bonsai is a Japanese word meaning “tray-planted”. It refers both to miniature trees in containers and to the art of training and growing them. Bonsai specimens are ordinary trees and shrubs, not hereditary dwarfs: they are dwarfed by pruning roots and branches, with shapes controlled by wiring the trunk and branches. The art originated in China more than 1,000 years ago and has been pursued and developed mainly by the Japanese.
facts: Bonsai specimens are ordinary trees and shrubs, not hereditary dwarfs; they are dwarfed by pruning roots and branches, and their shapes controlled by wiring the trunk and branches.
Bonsai originated in China more than 1,000 years ago, but it has been pursued and developed mainly by the Japanese.

In 1976 the people of Japan gave 53 bonsai and 6 viewing stones to the United States for the Bicentennial — 50 trees in honour of the 50 states, plus 3 from the Imperial family — founding the National Bonsai & Penjing Museum.

sources.title: U.S. National Arboretum Celebrates 50 Years of Bonsai

subjects.title: Cherry Blossom
subjects.summary: The flowering cherry, or sakura — a centuries-old symbol in Japanese culture, and a gift of friendship carried around the world.
subjects.description: In Japan, the flowering cherry tree, or sakura, is an important flowering plant, and the beauty of the cherry blossom is a symbol with rich meaning in Japanese culture. The tradition of celebrating the spring blooming of cherry trees in Japan is centuries old. In 1912, the people of Japan gave 3,020 cherry trees to the people of the United States as a gift of friendship, beginning a cycle of giving that continues today.
facts: The tradition of celebrating the blooming of cherry trees in Japan is centuries old.

On 26 March 1912, 3,020 cherry trees from twelve varieties arrived in Washington, DC, as a gift of friendship from the people of Japan — after a first shipment of 2,000 trees in 1910 was found diseased and burned.
The giving went both ways: in 1952, the National Park Service shipped budwood from descendants of the 1912 trees back to Tokyo to help restore the famed cherry grove along the Arakawa River.
